title: Unknown-caveat bypass
attack: Issue a mandate carrying a caveat key the verifier does not recognize, so the restriction it names is silently not enforced.
why: A verifier that skips keys it does not know treats an unknown restriction as no restriction. The mandate looks tighter than it is to a human reading it, and looser than it reads to the code enforcing it.
check: The registry is pinned by `v`. An unregistered key rejects the whole chain rather than being ignored, and the same rule applies inside `narrows` so a comparison involving an unknown key cannot return "narrower".

test.name: fails closed on unregistered keys
rejects an unregistered caveat key anywhere in the chain
an unregistered caveat key rejects the whole comparison

title: Grandchild escape past an omitted caveat
attack: A middle link omits a caveat the root declared; the grandchild re-declares it wider. Every parent-child pair narrows, so pairwise checking admits the chain.
why: Absence is ⊤. A link that simply says nothing about `settle` is unconstrained on that axis, so `escrow_schema → (omitted) → immediate` narrows at every step and widens overall. `narrows` is **not** pairwise transitive, which is the single least obvious thing about the lattice.
check: Each link is compared against the **accumulated meet** of everything above it, not against its immediate parent. Folding as the walk proceeds makes the relation transitive by construction and rejects the escape at the link that attempts it.

test.name: blocks the grandchild escape that pairwise checking would allow
blocks the same escape on resources
narrows is NOT pairwise transitive — an omitted caveat is ⊤
narrowing against the accumulated meet IS transitive

title: Widening by omitting a caveat
attack: Drop a caveat in a child mandate and hope the verifier reads absence as "unbounded".
why: Absence *is* ⊤ in the wire format — that uniformity is what the algebra rests on. What must not follow is that the effective authority forgets what an ancestor said.
check: The effective authority is the meet of the whole chain, so an omitted caveat is re-applied from above. A post-condition then re-checks that the fold narrows every individual link, turning a bug in `narrows` or `meet` from a silent escalation into a rejected chain.

test.name: re-applies a caveat the child omitted
a child cannot escape a parent caveat by omitting it
extending a chain never increases effective authority

title: Pattern widening via encoding
attack: Write a resource pattern or a request URI so that two strings compare as different but resolve to the same resource — percent-encoding, dot segments, case, default ports.
why: Comparing raw strings makes the grant depend on spelling. `%2e%2e/` looks like an ordinary path segment until something decodes it, and a verifier that resolves dot segments *before* decoding lets `/a/%2e%2e/b` escape a prefix it was supposed to be inside.
check: Canonicalize before comparing, and in the order that matters: decode first, then resolve dot segments. Patterns use a restricted grammar with no regex, so containment is decidable rather than approximate. An encoded slash stays encoded, because it is not a path separator.

test.name: decodes percent-escaped dot segments BEFORE resolving them
rejects regex-ish and multi-wildcard patterns
prefix matching does not leak across sibling paths
canonicalization is idempotent and never yields a traversal
rejects a resource outside the grant, including via traversal

title: Injecting an unrecognized top-level claim
attack: Add a top-level claim the verifier does not know, hoping it is ignored or acted on.
why: Anything a verifier ignores is a place to hide meaning that a *different* verifier might honour, and the two disagree about what the same bytes authorize.
check: Unknown top-level claims reject the chain, exactly as unknown caveats do.

test.name: rejects unknown top-level claims

title: Cross-currency comparison
attack: Present a request in a currency the mandate does not name and hope a comparison returns a convenient answer.
why: Comparing `5.00 USD` against `5.00 EUR` has no correct numeric answer, and a comparator that returns a boolean has already given the wrong one. Returning `false` for "not narrower" reads as a violation; returning `true` grants across currencies at an implied rate of 1.
check: Cross-currency comparison is a typed failure — `currency_mismatch` — not a boolean. No conversion is ever implied.

test.name: fails closed across currencies rather than returning false
rejects a request denominated differently from the mandate

title: Algorithm confusion
attack: Present a token whose header names an algorithm that turns a public key into a verification secret, or `alg: none`.
why: The whole JWT algorithm-confusion family comes from one mistake: letting `alg` *select* the key or the implementation. If the header can choose, the attacker chooses.
check: A static allowlist of one algorithm. The key comes from the resolver; `alg` only has to agree with it, and never selects anything.

test.name: rejects alg:none and unsigned tokens

title: Stolen mandate replayed
attack: Copy a mandate chain out of a log, a proxy, or a compromised host, and present it.
why: A credential that authorizes on presentation alone is a bearer token, and a leaked one is a blank cheque against the principal.
check: `cnf.jkt` at every link. The holder proves possession by signing the actual HTTP request (RFC 9421), and the verifier matches that key's thumbprint against the leaf's `cnf.jkt`.

test.name: binds the presenter key to the leaf cnf.jkt
binds proof of possession to the leaf holder
is refused by the ledger when the signing key is not the leaf holder

title: Forging or editing a link
attack: Extend a chain with a link the parent holder never signed, or edit a signed one.
why: Delegation is only as good as the rule about who may sign what. A verifier that checks each link against *any* trusted key, rather than against its parent's subject, lets any holder mint a sibling of any other.
check: Link *i* must be signed by the key named as link *i−1*'s `sub`, and `iss`/`par` must agree with the parent. The root, and only the root, is checked against the trusted-issuer set.

test.name: rejects a link signed by anyone but the parent holder
rejects a tampered payload
rejects an untrusted root issuer

title: Key compromise at depth *n*
attack: Compromise a subagent key and spend everything the principal has.
why: A delegation format where a leaf key can reach the root's authority has not delegated anything; it has shared a password.
check: Every link is independently PoP-bound to its own holder, and consumption debits the whole path, so a compromised key at depth *n* yields the authority of that subtree and no more. Short `exp` and subtree revocation bound the window.

test.name: revoking an ancestor stops every descendant
revoking a leaf leaves its sibling alone
reports the exhausted ancestor even when the leaf still has room

title: Delegating deeper than granted
attack: Delegate deeper than the grant allows, or reset the depth budget by omitting `depth` in a middle link.
why: `depth` is a counter, not an order. Treating omission as "unbounded" — the reading every other caveat gets — resets the budget at the first link that stays silent.
check: Each hop consumes one; omission inherits the remaining count rather than resetting it, and a link may only clamp it further. `delegable: false` seals a subtree outright.

test.name: consumes one depth per hop, and omission inherits rather than resetting
rejects delegation from a sealed mandate
enforces MAX_DEPTH

title: Clock skew abuse
attack: Present a chain outside its window and rely on the verifier's clock being generous, or on disagreement between two verifiers.
why: Unbounded skew tolerance turns `exp` into a suggestion. It matters most in offline mode, where `exp` is the only bound on revocation.
check: ±60s hard tolerance, and in online mode the Ledger's clock is authoritative rather than the merchant's or the agent's. The effective window is the intersection across every link, not the leaf's.

test.name: rejects an expired chain outside the skew tolerance
rejects a not-yet-valid chain
narrows the validity window structurally

title: Confused deputy
attack: A subagent reuses authority granted for one task to fund a different one.
why: Budget alone cannot tell the difference. A mandate that says "$50" and nothing else funds whatever the holder is currently being persuaded to do, which is the whole shape of a prompt-injection loss.
check: The `purpose` and `task` caveats, plus `task_id` bound into the presentation signature so the agent cannot relabel a request after the fact.

test.name: rejects a missing or ungranted purpose
pins the task when the grant does
enforces a per-task ceiling across separate mandates

title: Spend-token replay
attack: Capture a spend token in flight and present it again, or at a second merchant.
why: A spend token is a bearer instrument for its lifetime. Without a replay cache it pays as many times as it is presented.
check: Single use via a `jti` cache with a TTL of **2×** the token lifetime, `aud`-bound to one host, and an RFC 9421 signature covering the `Payment` header. The doubled TTL closes the skew-width window where a token is still acceptable but no longer remembered.

test.name: rejects a replayed jti
rejects a token addressed to another merchant
rejects a replayed token

title: Replay-cache poisoning
attack: Present a forged token — or one addressed elsewhere — carrying a `jti` you expect the real agent to use, so the legitimate presentation bounces as a replay.
why: A cache that records `jti` before validating the token lets anyone burn any identifier for free. The agent's real token is then refused, and the money is already debited at the Ledger.
check: **The order is normative.** The replay check runs after signature and audience verification, so a token nobody could have issued never reaches the cache.

test.name: does not let an unsigned or misaddressed token burn a legitimate jti
does not let an unsigned request burn the token

title: Signature covering nothing useful
attack: Sign an RFC 9421 covered-component list that omits the parts that matter, then reuse that signature on a different request.
why: A signature over `@method` alone verifies perfectly and constrains nothing. The verifier that checks "is there a valid signature" rather than "does it cover what I care about" has bought itself a decoration.
check: The merchant checks the *declared* covered-component list actually contains `@method`, `@target-uri` and `payment`, and rejects the request if not.

test.name: rejects a signature that does not cover the payment header
rejects a signature lifted onto a different URL
rejects a signature lifted onto a different method
rejects a swapped payment token

title: Token lifted to a pricier endpoint
attack: Take a token minted for a cheap endpoint and spend it on an expensive one within its 60-second window.
why: The token names an amount, and an endpoint that only checks the amount is happy to be underpaid for something dearer.
check: The merchant compares `token.res` against the canonical request URI, and the amount against the *current* price for that resource — not against whatever the token says it is worth.

test.name: rejects a token minted for another resource
rejects a token whose amount does not match the current price

title: Merchant learns the delegation tree
attack: A merchant learns the principal's delegation tree, budgets and org structure from the credential it is handed.
why: Presenting the chain to the merchant would be the simplest design, and it discloses every ancestor's budget and identity to a counterparty that needs to know only "this is paid for".
check: The merchant never sees the chain. The spend token carries `chain_hash`, which commits to the authority that produced it without disclosing it.

test.name: never shows the merchant the mandate chain

title: `jti` re-issue to reset a budget
attack: Re-sign a mandate reusing a `jti` that has already been spent against, with a fresh `max_total`. Every signature is valid and every caveat narrows.
why: The `jti` is the key for consumption state, so a Ledger that keys a counter by `jti` and trusts whatever content arrives with it has just been told the budget is full again. The signature chain alone does not prevent this — nothing in §7 is violated.
check: The Ledger stores a hash of the link's JWS at materialization and rejects a later presentation of the same `jti` with different content.

test.name: rejects a jti reused with different content
is idempotent, and refuses a jti re-presented with different content

title: Overdraw on a mandate's first concurrent spends
attack: Fire several spends concurrently against a mandate that has never been used.
why: The obvious implementation takes `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the path's rows. **A row that does not exist locks nothing**, and a mandate's first spend has no row — so every concurrent first spend reads `spent = 0`, and the last write wins instead of adding. Overdraw on the first two calls against any new mandate, not in some rare interleaving.
check: Nodes are locked by *key*, not by row: a transaction-scoped advisory lock exists before the row does, and is taken in the same root-to-leaf order.

test.name: debits every one of several concurrent first spends on a fresh mandate

title: Deadlock as a denial of service
attack: Drive ordinary concurrent traffic and rely on mixed lock ordering to wedge the ledger.
why: Not adversarial at all, which is the point. Every spend under a principal touches the same root, so paths overlap constantly; two transactions locking overlapping rows in different orders deadlock under normal load.
check: Locks are taken root-to-leaf, always, and the ordering lives in `lockPath` rather than in the direction a caller happens to write a loop. Any consistent global order would do; this one is deadlock-free because every path shares a prefix from the root.

test.name: holds for interleaved reserves across two siblings
conserves funds across interleaved reserve, settle and refund

title: Sibling collusion
attack: Two subagents under one principal each spend their full allowance, jointly exceeding what the principal granted.
why: Enforcing a budget at the leaf alone makes the principal's ceiling the *sum* of its children rather than the number it wrote down.
check: Consumption debits the whole path. Every ancestor must independently afford a spend, so joint spend is bounded by the common ancestor.

test.name: bounds sibling collusion by the common ancestor
debits every ancestor, not just the leaf
holds the task ceiling across two principals sharing a task

title: Spending one mandate at every ledger
attack: Present the same chain to several Ledgers. Each verifies it, each accepts it, each debits its own state — so a `max_total` of 20.00 buys 20.00 at every Ledger that will take it.
why: §7 step 3 says "all links agree on `ledger`", which *reads* like it binds a chain to one Ledger and does not. Agreement among the links makes a chain internally coherent; it says nothing about who is reading it. Consumption state is per-Ledger, so a second Ledger that accepts the chain offers a second full budget — and nothing in §7 is violated along the way, because every signature is valid, every caveat narrows, and every link does agree. The natural implementation uses its own URL only as the `iss` of minted spend tokens and never compares it to anything, which is exactly what this one did.
check: The second half of §7 step 3, enforced in `verifyChain` itself so it binds every party that acts on a chain rather than only the one that noticed first. `VerifyOptions.ledger` is **required**, and declining the check is the `ANY_LEDGER` sentinel rather than an omitted field — the failure mode of this rule is that somebody forgets it, so an absent parameter and a deliberate opt-out must not look alike. Three parties are bound: a Ledger at `reserve` and at `register`, and an **offline** merchant, which is the one that settles with no Ledger on the path and is therefore the only party acting on the chain at all. `register` needs it independently — the status list URI is derived as `{ledger}/v1/status/{root}`, so registering a foreign chain mints an index no merchant will ever fetch and records the mandate as revocable when it is not.

test.name: refuses a chain addressed to another ledger
refuses even when every link agrees — agreement is not address
does not let one mandate be spent in full at every ledger that takes it
refuses to register one either — a list nobody would fetch is worse than none
refuses a conforming chain addressed to another ledger
is what stops an offline spend that would debit no ledger at all

title: Retry-storm griefing
attack: Loop against a cheap endpoint. A $0.05 call burns $500 overnight while nobody is watching.
why: Autonomous spend fails catastrophically rather than gradually. Nothing about a retry loop looks anomalous per-call — only the rate does, and only against a baseline.
check: `rate` enforced at every ancestor independently, plus velocity and burn-rate breakers against a rolling baseline, plus a per-task ceiling.

test.name: enforces an ancestor rate the leaf never declared
blocks a velocity anomaly against the rolling baseline
never lets a rate caveat be exceeded within its window

title: Refunds used to reset a rate limit
attack: Spend, get refunded, repeat — using refunds to reset a rate limit.
why: A refund restores money, so the obvious implementation restores the rate counter with it. But `rate` bounds *how often the agent acts*, and an action that was taken and reversed still happened. Crediting the counter turns "5 per hour" into "unlimited, as long as they fail".
check: A refund credits budget and does **not** credit the rate counter. The two are different quantities and only one of them is money.

test.name: credits budget on refund but not the rate counter

title: Agent approving its own step-up
attack: Read the `step_up_required` error, take the approval handle out of it, and present it back on the retry.
why: The Ledger hands the handle to the agent. Treating possession of it as consent means the party being restrained lifts its own restraint — and `step_up` is the only mechanism in the protocol for keeping a high-value transaction attended. This implementation did exactly this, and the test asserting it called re-presenting the handle "once approved".
check: A handle records that a *question was asked*. The approval is a separate signed answer from the mandate's trusted root issuer, restating `root`, `res` and `amt` so the signature attests to terms rather than to an opaque string. Only `state: approved` admits a spend, exactly once.

test.name: does not accept its own handle back as approval
refuses a decision signed by anyone but the principal
refuses a decision whose signed terms do not match the request
refuses a decision signed by the agent, however it is submitted

title: Redirecting a signed step-up decision
attack: Take a decision the principal signed for one request and submit it against another.
why: A signature over a bare handle attests only that the principal saw an opaque identifier; it cannot distinguish the request they were shown from any other. Routing by URL path rather than by signed content lets the path and the signature disagree.
check: The decision restates the terms and the Ledger re-checks all three against its own record before honouring it. The path/signature mismatch is caught before the decision is applied, not after.

test.name: will not let the path redirect a signed decision onto another request
honours a denial and does not let the agent retry into a yes

title: Replaying a captured `release`
attack: Capture a signed `release` and replay it at the next incident, un-halting a principal who deliberately halted.
why: A control action names no one-shot handle, so nothing else prevents replay. A replayed `kill` is harmless; a replayed `release` is not, and an agent that captured one only has to wait. An in-memory nonce cache is insufficient — a halted principal is precisely the situation likely to involve a restart.
check: Every decision carries a `jti` the Ledger consumes exactly once, **durably**, in the same transaction that applies the action.

test.name: consumes a decision exactly once

title: One principal halting another
attack: On a Ledger serving several principals, sign a kill or revoke naming someone else's root.
why: `isTrustedRootIssuer` answers "is this DID *a* principal we trust", not "is this DID *this subtree's* principal". Checking only the trust list lets any tenant halt any other. Making the check possible at all required the Ledger to start recording who issued each mandate.
check: The decision's `iss` is checked against the **root node's recorded issuer**, and a `revoke` target must be in that root's subtree.

test.name: will not let one principal halt another principal
revokes a mandate in its own subtree and refuses one outside it
still refuses a revoke naming a target under a different root it has seen

title: Using the control endpoint from the agent's network
attack: Reach the control or approval endpoint from the agent's own network and use it.
why: The network the kill switch most needs to be reachable from is the agent's. An endpoint protected by a bearer secret is protected by something the agent may well be holding.
check: Control and step-up decisions carry their own authority as signatures, so the endpoint needs no auth of its own and reaching it is not the same as being allowed to use it. The **read** side has no such excuse and is documented as needing the deployment's own access control.

test.name: accepts a signed control action over HTTP and refuses an unsigned one

title: Spending a mandate revoked before its first use
attack: Spend a mandate the principal already revoked, by never having spent it before.
why: Consumption state materializes on first presentation, so a Ledger that stores revocation *on that state* has nowhere to put a revocation for a mandate it has not seen. This implementation refused such a revocation as "unknown mandate", and the first spend then created the node unrevoked and went through — a window covering the mandate's entire life up to its first use.
check: Revocation is a record of its own, independent of materialization, and a node created later inherits it. It is keyed by root because an unmaterialized `jti` has no recorded parent to check a subtree claim against.

test.name: revokes a jti with no node at all, and the node materializes revoked
does not let one principal pre-revoke a jti under another principal
records a revocation for a jti with no node, scoped to its root

title: Status-list rollback un-revoking a mandate
attack: Serve a merchant an older status list that has not yet expired, un-revoking everything revoked since.
why: `exp` does not stop this. The older list is a perfectly valid, correctly signed, in-date document — nothing about it is malformed. Freshness bounds how *old* a list may be, not whether it is the *latest*.
check: A consumer refuses any `seq` below one it has already accepted for that `sub`. `seq` counts revocations, so it rises monotonically and a lagging replica is refused too.

test.name: refuses a rollback to a still-valid older list
will not go backwards even if the network serves an older list
numbers a list by what is revoked in it, not by when it was built

title: Status list pinned to hide a revocation
attack: Answer the status fetch — from a cache, a proxy, or the path — with yesterday's list, forever.
why: A status list with no expiry is a document, not a mechanism. Whoever answers the fetch decides when revocation stops propagating, and nothing in the list itself contradicts them.
check: `exp` is mandatory, a stale list is refused rather than served, and the served `Cache-Control: max-age` tracks the list's own remaining lifetime so an intermediary cannot hold it longer than the signature commits to.

test.name: refuses a list that has expired, with no fallback to serving it anyway
keeps serving the cached list when a refresh fails, until it expires
caps how long an intermediary may hold a list to the list's own lifetime

title: Status list as a decompression bomb
attack: Answer the status fetch with a few kilobytes of gzip that expand to gigabytes.
why: The list is compressed and fetched over a network, so `gunzip` runs on attacker-reachable input. A verifier that decompresses in order to see what it has is a memory-exhaustion primitive with a signature check bolted on afterwards.
check: The signature is verified **before** anything is decompressed, so only the Ledger can cause an inflation at all; the signed `bits` then caps that inflation. A payload that decompresses to any other length is refused — short included, because a truncated bitstring reads as "nothing is revoked".

test.name: checks the signature before it decompresses anything
refuses a payload that decompresses past its declared size
refuses a payload that decompresses short of its declared size

title: Blocking the status fetch to bypass the check
attack: Break the merchant's status-list fetch, so revocation cannot be checked and every revoked mandate works again.
why: If "I could not check" is treated as "not revoked", then causing an outage *is* the bypass — and causing an outage is much easier than forging a list.
check: A chain carrying `st` that cannot be checked is refused with `status_unknown` (503, not 403 — "I could not find out" is not "this is revoked"). A cache whose refresh is failing keeps serving what it has until that list's own `exp`, and then starts refusing.

test.name: refuses a listed mandate when the list cannot be consulted at all
keeps serving the cached list when a refresh fails, until it expires

title: Pointing a status list at a host the issuer controls
attack: Issue a mandate whose status list lives at a host the issuer controls, and answer "not revoked" forever.
why: Any credential that names where to check its own revocation has handed that decision to whoever issued it. The natural design — a `status_uri` claim — is exactly this.
check: The URI is **derived**, never declared: `{ledger}/v1/status/{root_jti}`, from the `ledger` claim every link already agrees on plus the head of the path. There is nothing left to point elsewhere.

test.name: derives the list URI from the chain rather than from a claim
asks for the list at the URI derived from the chain
refuses a list for a different root or a different ledger

title: Two mandates sharing a status index
attack: Allocate one status index to two mandates, so revoking one does not revoke the mandate that matters.
why: Allocation is the issuer's job and issuers have bugs. The dangerous half is the publisher: walking nodes and writing `bit[idx] = node.revoked` lets the unrevoked mandate clear the revoked one's bit, depending on nothing but row order.
check: The list is built as the **union** of revoked indices, which cannot express a clear. A collision then costs an unnecessary refusal instead of a missed one — the direction a revocation mechanism has to fail in.

test.name: builds by union, so a shared index never clears a revoked bit

title: Idempotency key reused for a different request
attack: Reuse an idempotency key with a different request, to be handed someone else's reservation — or your own earlier one — for a spend you did not make.
why: The obliging implementation returns the first response for a repeated key. That silently tells a caller something went through that never did, which is worse than either debiting again or failing.
check: The key is bound to a hash of the chain, the request and the quote. A key reused with a different request is refused, not answered. Refusals are recorded too, including `step_up_required`, so a replay returns the same handle rather than queueing the question twice.

test.name: refuses a key reused for a different request
replays a refusal rather than re-deciding it
returns the same step-up handle on replay rather than queueing twice

title: Idempotency hash collision via encoding
attack: Craft two different requests that hash to one idempotency key, and be handed the other caller's reservation.
why: Node's `'ascii'` encoding is latin1-equivalent on encode: it truncates code points above U+00FF modulo 256. `Ł` (U+0141) becomes byte 0x41, which is `A` — so `/Łedger` and `/Aedger` hash identically. The JWS hash beside it may legitimately use `'ascii'`, because base64url is ASCII by construction, which is exactly why the wrong one is easy to copy.
check: The request hash is taken over UTF-8. Only the token hash, whose input is base64url, uses `ascii`.

test.name: does not collide two requests that differ only above U+00FF

title: Double transfer after a crash
attack: Crash the Ledger between paying a rail and recording that it paid, then let the retry pay again.
why: Paying and recording are two writes to two systems. Any crash between them either double-pays or strands the money, and which one you get depends on the order you chose.
check: The rail idempotency key is derived from the spend `jti`, so a retry of the same reservation is the same transfer to the rail rather than a second one. The nonce comes from the `spendId`, never from randomness.

test.name: never pays twice for one reservation
derives the nonce from the spendId, not from randomness
is idempotent for a given spendId

title: Refund-on-timeout draining a principal
attack: Make settlement time out repeatedly. If a timeout refunds, the budget is restored while the money may already have moved — spend the same allowance again.
why: Settlement has **three** outcomes, not two: success, terminal failure, and *indeterminate*. Collapsing the third into either neighbour costs a double-spend or a stranded balance, depending on which way you guess, and a timeout is the most common indeterminate there is.
check: An indeterminate settlement stays `settling` and stays debited until a reconciler asks the rail what actually happened. Escalation moves no money; it changes only who knows.

test.name: holds an indeterminate settlement rather than guessing
leaves an undecided payment debited and waiting
never sweeps a reservation still in flight with the rail
treats a 5xx after payment as INDETERMINATE

title: Refunding a failed irreversible call, then retrying it
attack: Call an irreversible tool, have it report an error, collect the refund, and call it again — funding two orders on one allowance.
why: A tool that reports failure has not proved it had no effect. Refunding a failed order is exactly how an agent retries a trade it already placed, and the JSON-RPC error looks identical either way.
check: Refund by `effect`, not by outcome: a failed `read` refunds because a failed read did nothing; a failed `write` or `irreversible` **settles**; a transport failure holds the reservation for reconciliation.

test.name: consumes the allowance when an irreversible tool fails
holds the reservation when the transport dies mid-call
consumes the allowance when an irreversible tool fails

title: Free service via precision truncation
attack: Price a call below the rail's smallest representable unit and have it round to zero — free service, at scale.
why: Per-call pricing runs below a tenth of a cent, and rails carry a fixed number of atomic units. Rounding is the obliging behaviour and it is the bug: a sub-precision amount is not a small payment, it is no payment.
check: Conversion at the asset's precision is exact. An amount below it is a **terminal** failure, never rounded, and money never touches binary floating point anywhere in the codebase.

test.name: refuses to round away precision the rail cannot carry
treats sub-precision amounts as terminal, not as free
compares exactly where floats would not
honours sub-cent precision exactly

title: Releasing escrow without a verdict
attack: Settle an `escrow_schema` reservation without ever producing the verdict escrow exists to wait for.
why: Escrow that releases on a timer, or on the agent saying so, is not escrow. The verdict is the entire mechanism.
check: A reservation under `escrow_schema` will not settle without a verdict, and refunds when the response fails validation. `escrow_human` holds until a human approves.

test.name: escrow_schema will not settle without a verdict
escrow_schema refunds when the response fails validation
escrow_human holds until approved

title: Settling one reservation twice
attack: Settle one reservation twice, or settle one a sweeper is concurrently refunding.
why: Both are read-then-write on the same row. Without a lock that covers the read, two callers see `reserved` and both pay.
check: Settling claims the reservation by moving it off `reserved` inside the transaction that reads it, and the sweeper takes the same lock before crediting.

test.name: refuses to settle the same reservation twice
does not sweep a reservation that is mid-settlement
never sweeps a reservation still in flight with the rail

title: Agent redirects a non-custodial payment
attack: Take a directive the Ledger issued and sign a transfer to a different recipient, amount, or asset.
why: In non-custodial mode the agent holds the signing key. If the directive is advice rather than a commitment, the agent decides where the money goes and the Ledger finds out afterwards.
check: The directive pins every field of the transfer and is signed by the Ledger; the agent-side signer verifies that signature, checks the directive is bound to its own key, and computes the digest itself rather than accepting one. `directive_hash` is compared again on report.

test.name: pins every field of the transfer
rejects an intent that does not match its own hash
rejects one bound to another agent key
computes the digest itself rather than accepting one
rejects an instruction that does not match its directive

title: Agent falsely reports payment
attack: Report a directive as executed without executing it, or with someone else's signature.
why: The report comes from the party with the incentive to lie. Any settlement that trusts it is settling on the agent's say-so.
check: Settlement is confirmed by reading the chain — `authorizationState` — never by the report. A proof signed by the wrong key, or over a different authorization, refunds immediately.

test.name: accepts a proof that matches the directive, and still does not settle
refunds immediately when the proof was signed by someone else
settles only once the authorization is actually consumed
settles a directive the agent executed but never reported

title: Nonce reused for a different transfer
attack: Get the signer to reuse an authorization nonce for a different transfer, so one on-chain slot covers two intents.
why: EIP-3009 nonces are the replay defence. A signer that derives one from randomness cannot be idempotent; a signer that reuses one across differing intents has broken the defence.
check: The nonce is derived from the `spendId`, so re-requesting an identical transfer is idempotent, and requesting a *different* transfer under the same nonce is refused.

test.name: is idempotent for an identical re-request
refuses to re-use a nonce for a different transfer

title: Exfiltrating the agent signing key
attack: Get the signing key out of the agent process through a log line, an error path, a JSON dump, or a debugger repr.
why: Keys leak through the mundane: `JSON.stringify` on a config object, an exception carrying its context, `util.inspect` in a crash handler. A key held as an ordinary property is one careless log away from a transcript.
check: The key never leaves the closure — not reachable as a property, redacted in JSON and `inspect` output, and not present in policy-refusal or audit paths.

test.name: is redacted in JSON and inspect output
is not reachable as a property
does not leak the key through a policy refusal
calls the audit hook on success without exposing the key

title: Agent bypasses the Ledger entirely
attack: In non-custodial mode, simply sign a transfer that no directive ever authorized.
why: The agent holds the key. Nothing in a protocol can stop a key-holder signing, which is the honest statement the alternative designs avoid making.
check: **Not preventable non-custodially.** Detected by reconciling the payer account against issued directives. The preventive answer requires co-signing or custody, and both have costs the spec declines to hide — see open question 9.

test.name: declares its weaker capabilities honestly

gap: Detective only, and the reconciliation it depends on is not implemented here — `DelegatedTransferRail` declares the weaker guarantees, but nothing in this repo watches a payer account. Stated rather than engineered around.

title: Treating a rail as more decidable than it is
attack: Treat a rail that cannot prove settlement as though it could, and auto-refund on its silence.
why: Rails differ in what they can decide. An oracle-backed rail eventually answers; a card-shaped one may never. Applying one policy to both means either refunding payments that landed or holding ones that never will.
check: A rail declares its capabilities, and reconciliation escalates rather than refunding where the rail gives no guarantee that it will ever decide. Expiry deadline and decidability deadline are separate.

test.name: declares its weaker capabilities honestly
separates the expiry deadline from the decidability deadline
ESCALATES instead of refunding, because a late settlement is still possible
reports a rail-raised escalation to the pager

title: Cross-merchant parallel spend
attack: Present the same offline mandate to several merchants at once, before any of them reports consumption.
why: Offline mode's whole premise is that the merchant settles without contacting the Ledger, so nothing is authoritative at spend time. Parallel presentation is not a flaw in the mechanism; it is the price of it.
check: Online, the Ledger is authoritative and this cannot happen. Offline, loss is **bounded** rather than prevented, and only by all the constraints together: one non-wildcard host in `aud`, `max_total` present and therefore scoped to it, `exp` − `nbf` ≤ 1 hour, `settle: immediate`. `verifyChain({ offline: true })` holds a chain to all four as one check, against the *effective* authority rather than any single link. The fifth — reporting consumption every 60 seconds — is a property of a deployment, not a credential.

test.name: refuses a wildcard audience, which names a set rather than a merchant
refuses a window over an hour, to the second
refuses escrow, and refuses leaving settle unconstrained
admits a conforming chain and refuses one that is merely valid
checks the fold, not any one link
sums worst-case exposure per merchant

gap: Bounded, never prevented — that is what §13 buys and it is the whole trade. `offlineRiskBudget` computes the figure §13 says MUST be surfaced to the principal, but nothing in this repo *tracks* live offline grants to feed it, and the 60-second reporting requirement is not enforced anywhere either. A deployment has to wire both.

title: Calling a tool the enforcement layer cannot price
attack: Call a tool the gateway has no price for, and spend nothing against the mandate while doing it.
why: A gateway that prices what it knows and forwards the rest is a spending control with a hole shaped like every tool nobody configured.
check: The gateway refuses what it cannot price, and goes further: `tools/list` is the mandate rendered, so unpriced and unpermitted tools are never shown. An agent cannot misuse what it was never offered.

test.name: hides unpriced tools rather than refusing them later
hides what the mandate does not permit
completes the handshake and lists only priced tools

title: Reaching the upstream server without the gateway
attack: Configure the upstream MCP server directly alongside the gateway, and call it without a mandate.
why: The gateway constrains a **channel**, not an agent. Its preventive property holds exactly as long as the client reaches the upstream only through it.
check: None available at this layer. Stated plainly in the module and the README rather than engineered around; the harness hook covers a different surface, and neither is a sandbox.
gap: Structural, not fixable inside the gateway. A deployment that needs this guarantee needs egress control or a sandbox, which this project does not provide and does not claim to.

title: Ledger outage as unmetered spending
attack: Make the ledger unreachable, so the enforcement layer fails open and every priced call runs unmetered.
why: An enforcement point in front of a network dependency has to choose. Allowing on error is the one that keeps the demo working and is indistinguishable from having no control at all for the length of the outage.
check: The harness hook denies by default when the ledger cannot be reached. A deployment that would rather take the other risk has to say so explicitly.

test.name: refuses by default, because unmetered spending is the failure it exists to prevent
can be told to allow instead, but only deliberately

title: A refusal mistaken for a transport error
attack: Not an attack — a failure mode with the same effect. An agent wraps its calls in `try/catch`, a spending refusal arrives as an exception, and the retry loop turns a budget control into a hot loop.
why: `fetch` throws on network failure, so a drop-in replacement that throws on refusal teaches every existing caller to retry a decision that will never change.
check: A refusal is a `Response` carrying RFC 9457 problem details and an `x-am-refusal` header with the §15 code, so "your principal said no" is distinguishable from "the merchant said no" and from a transport failure. Network failures still throw, because that is what `fetch` does.

test.name: returns problem details rather than throwing when the budget is gone
marks its own refusals so they are not mistaken for the merchant s
relays a ledger refusal as a refusal, not as a transport error

title: Stale or mutated 402 quote replay
attack: Present a spend token minted from an expired, repriced, lifted, or mutated 402 challenge, or settle an x402 payment after the storefront silently swapped payTo or terms.
why: Without cryptographic quote binding, `quote_id` is an unchecked label: a spend token remains valid for its own TTL after the quote expires or the resource reprices, and a custodial x402 rail that only compares amounts misses `payTo` or domain mutations.
check: Domain-separated SHA-256 `quote_hash` binds canonical URI and exact 402 challenge bytes into reservations, spend tokens, directives, and receipts. Merchants with `QuoteStore` or `requireQuoteBinding` enforce single-use, expiry, digest, price, schema, and settle-mode equality; x402 rails verify the digest before signing or preparing directives.

test.name: rejects a stale cheap quote after the merchant reprices the resource
rejects an expired quote even when the spend token and signature are fresh
refuses custodial x402 settlement and refunds when live PAYMENT-REQUIRED mutates payTo or amount
binds verbatim PAYMENT-REQUIRED header in non-custodial X402NonCustodialRail directive

title: Org topology leaked via receipt `path`
attack: Inspect signed receipts shared with merchants or external verifiers to read cleartext internal mandate names or reconstruct department and subagent delegation hierarchies.
why: Cleartext `path` arrays hand the org chart to anyone who reads a receipt, undercutting the §1.1 claim that merchants learn nothing about the principal delegation tree.
check: Optional `receiptPathPrivacy` modes encode `path` and `principal` using keyed HMAC-SHA256 with a minimum 16-byte secret salt: `salted` hides cleartext mandate ids while preserving O(1) indexed subtree rollup, and `blinded` salts per `spend` id so external readers cannot cluster spends across receipts.

test.name: hides cleartext mandate JTIs and principal while preserving indexed subtree rollup
produces unlinkable path and principal tags across spends under the same subtree while allowing salted audit
rejects a receipt privacy salt shorter than 16 bytes

title: Unbounded mandate or total substitution across AP2 / ACP interop
attack: Feed an AP2 IntentMandate without a cap, drop user cart confirmation or refundability during translation, or reprice an ACP checkout session between authorization and completion.
why: Interop adapters are trust boundaries. Treating missing external fields as unconstrained `am/1` caveats turns a narrow external intent into an unbounded mandate, and submitting ACP `complete` without checking the session total lets a merchant charge more than the Ledger reserved.
check: AP2 and ACP inbound adapters fail closed on missing caps, expired timestamps, wildcard merchants, unconfirmed carts (`step_up: { over: 0 }`), and refundability downgrades (`immediate` refused). Outbound `AcpRail` refuses sub-minor-unit rounding, verifies the checkout session currency and total before `POST /complete`, and reconciles indeterminate completions via `GET /checkout_sessions/{id}`.

test.name: refuses to mint an unbounded mandate when AP2 IntentMandate omits a cap
enforces step-up in Ledger when AP2 IntentMandate requires user cart confirmation
refuses immediate settlement when AP2 IntentMandate requires refundability
refuses ACP completion when merchant reprices the checkout session total
holds indeterminate ACP 5xx completion in settling and reconciles via session status

title: Ledger compromise
attack: Compromise the Ledger and mint whatever spend tokens you like.
why: The Ledger holds the key that merchants verify against and the state that bounds every spend. There is no check downstream of it.
check: **None that prevents it.** Ledger keys MUST be HSM-backed. Receipts are dual-signed, so the transaction history can be reconstructed from merchant records independently of the Ledger — which is detection and reconstruction, not prevention.

test.name: is signed by the ledger over canonical bytes
canonicalizes independent of key order

gap: Full compromise of the principal's funds, stated as residual risk in §16 rather than mitigated. Nothing in this repo enforces HSM-backed keys or runs the independent reconciliation that would detect it.
